question: Which of the following is a store of energy?
A ball is thrown upwards. As it rises, which energy transfer occurs?
What is the unit of power?
A machine has a total input energy of 500 J and a useful output energy of 350 J. What is its efficiency?
Which of the following would increase the efficiency of a motor?
What does specific heat capacity tell us?
options: The energy needed to melt 1 kg of a substance
The energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C
The rate at which a substance loses heat
The temperature at which a substance boils
correct: The energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C

question: Which of the following is a renewable energy resource?
What is a disadvantage of solar energy?
options: It only generates electricity when the sun is shining
correct: It only generates electricity when the sun is shining

question: A force of 20 N moves an object 5 m. How much work is done?
Which statement best describes the conservation of energy?
options: Energy is created when fuel is burned
Energy can be destroyed when it becomes heat
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores
Useful energy is always greater than input energy
correct: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores

question: Which energy resource uses the gravitational potential energy of water?
A stretched spring stores energy in which store?
Where does wasted energy usually end up?
options: Back in the input energy store
Dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings
correct: Dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings

question: What is a disadvantage of fossil fuels?
options: They produce greenhouse gases contributing to climate change
They are very expensive to extract
They only work in sunny conditions
correct: They produce greenhouse gases contributing to climate change

question: A device transfers 600 J of energy in 2 minutes. What is its power output?
Energy cannot be created or destroyed — this is the law of conservation of __________.
Work done = force × __________.
Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ __________ input energy.
The energy needed to raise 1 kg of a material by 1°C is called its specific __________ capacity.
Coal, oil and natural gas are examples of __________ fuels.
An energy resource that will not run out is described as __________.
Power is measured in __________, where 1 unit equals 1 joule per second.
The spreading of energy into the surroundings as thermal energy is called __________.
A moving object has __________ energy.
The network that distributes electricity across the country is called the National __________.
Match each energy store to its correct description.

pairs.definition: Energy due to an object's motion
Energy due to an object's height above the ground
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed object
Energy stored in the bonds of chemical substances
Energy stored due to the motion of particles

question: Match each energy resource to whether it is renewable or non-renewable.

pairs.definition: Renewable — will not run out
Non-renewable — will eventually run out
Renewable — replenished by the sun
Non-renewable — uses uranium which is finite
Renewable — uses the water cycle

question: Match each equation to its correct quantity.

pairs.definition: Energy needed to heat a substance
Work done by a force
Power — rate of energy transfer
Kinetic energy of a moving object

question: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.definition: Useful output energy ÷ total input energy
Energy spreading into surroundings as thermal energy
Reducing friction to decrease wasted energy
Energy transferred to an unwanted store

question: Match each renewable energy source to how it generates electricity.

pairs.definition: Uses kinetic energy of moving air
Converts light energy directly into electricity
Uses gravitational potential energy of water
Uses kinetic energy of tidal water movement

question: State the principle of conservation of energy.
mark_scheme: Energy cannot be created or destroyed (1); it can only be transferred from one store to another (1) — accept either point.

question: State what is meant by the term efficiency.
mark_scheme: The proportion of input energy that is usefully transferred (1) / useful output ÷ total input (1) — accept either.

question: Name two renewable energy resources.
mark_scheme: Any two from: wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal, wave, geothermal, biomass (1 mark each) — 2 marks total.

question: A force of 50 N moves an object 8 m. Calculate the work done.
Explain why no machine is 100% efficient.
mark_scheme: Some energy is always transferred to unwanted stores (1); usually as thermal energy due to friction / sound (1); this energy is dissipated to the surroundings (1) — any two.

question: Describe the energy transfers that occur when a ball is dropped from a height.
mark_scheme: Gravitational potential energy decreases (1); kinetic energy increases as ball falls (1); on hitting the ground, kinetic energy transferred to thermal/sound energy (1) — any two.

question: Calculate the energy needed to heat 2 kg of water by 10°C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg°C.
Compare the environmental impact of fossil fuels and wind energy.
mark_scheme: Fossil fuels release CO₂ / greenhouse gases contributing to climate change (1); wind energy produces no greenhouse gases / carbon emissions (1); wind turbines may affect wildlife / landscape (1) — any two.

question: Explain why countries are increasing their use of renewable energy resources.
mark_scheme: Fossil fuels are non-renewable and will eventually run out (1); fossil fuels produce greenhouse gases / CO₂ causing climate change (1); renewable resources will not run out (1); renewable resources produce little or no greenhouse gases (1); advances in technology have reduced costs (1) — any three.

question: Describe how you would determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block in the laboratory.
mark_scheme: Heat the metal block using an immersion heater (1); measure the temperature change using a thermometer (1); measure the energy supplied using a joulemeter / calculate using P × t (1); use E = mcΔT to calculate specific heat capacity (1); insulate the block to reduce energy losses (1) — any three.

question: Explain three ways in which the efficiency of a car engine can be increased.
mark_scheme: Lubricate moving parts to reduce friction (1); use more aerodynamic design to reduce air resistance (1); use regenerative braking to recover kinetic energy (1); use lighter materials to reduce mass (1) — any three.

question: Evaluate the use of nuclear power as an energy resource. Include advantages and disadvantages in your answer.
mark_scheme: Advantages: produces large amounts of electricity (1); no greenhouse gas emissions during operation (1); reliable — not dependent on weather (1). Disadvantages: produces radioactive waste that is difficult to dispose of (1); risk of accidents e.g. Chernobyl / Fukushima (1); high cost to build and decommission (1); uses non-renewable uranium fuel (1) — any four.

question: A rollercoaster starts from rest at the top of a hill. Explain the energy transfers that take place as it travels down the hill and comes to a stop at the bottom.
mark_scheme: At the top: large gravitational potential energy store (1); as it descends GPE decreases and kinetic energy increases (1); some energy transferred to thermal energy by friction (1); at the bottom kinetic energy is greatest (1); brakes transfer kinetic energy to thermal energy (1) — any four.

question: A 3 kg block of aluminium is heated using a 50 W heater for 5 minutes. The temperature rises from 20°C to 80°C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium and suggest why your answer may differ from the accepted value.
mark_scheme: Energy supplied = P × t = 50 × 300 = 15 000 J (1); E = mcΔT → c = E ÷ (m × ΔT) = 15 000 ÷ (3 × 60) (1) = 83.3 J/kg°C (1); answer differs because energy is lost to surroundings / block not perfectly insulated (1).

question: Explain how the National Grid distributes electricity efficiently across the country.
mark_scheme: Power stations generate electricity at low voltage (1); transformers step up the voltage for transmission (1); high voltage means low current (1); lower current means less energy wasted as heat in cables (1); step-down transformers reduce voltage for safe use in homes (1) — any four.

question: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of wind energy as a replacement for fossil fuels.
mark_scheme: Advantages: renewable — will not run out (1); no greenhouse gas emissions during operation (1); low running costs once built (1); can be built offshore (1). Disadvantages: intermittent — only generates when wind blows (1); visual and noise pollution (1); large areas of land needed (1); expensive to build and maintain (1); may harm birds / wildlife (1) — any five.

question: The UK needs to meet its energy demands while reducing carbon emissions. Evaluate the options available, including both renewable and non-renewable sources, and suggest which combination of energy resources the UK should use.
mark_scheme: Fossil fuels are reliable but produce CO₂ / contribute to climate change (1); nuclear is reliable with no CO₂ emissions but produces radioactive waste (1); wind and solar are clean but intermittent (1); hydroelectric is reliable and renewable but limited locations (1); combination of sources provides reliability and reduces emissions (1); energy storage (batteries) needed to deal with intermittency (1); energy conservation also important to reduce demand (1); accept any well-reasoned suggestion for UK energy mix with justification (1) — any six.

question: A student investigates the efficiency of a motor lifting a weight. The motor uses 200 J of electrical energy to lift a 5 kg weight by 3 m. Explain how to calculate the efficiency of the motor and suggest reasons why it is less than 100%.
mark_scheme: GPE gained = mgh = 5 × 10 × 3 = 150 J (1); efficiency = useful output ÷ total input = 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75 or 75% (1); efficiency is less than 100% because some energy is wasted (1); wasted as thermal energy due to friction in motor (1); wasted as sound energy (1); energy dissipated to surroundings (1); cannot be recovered for useful work (1) — any six.

question: Explain how energy is transferred by conduction in a metal rod when one end is heated.
mark_scheme: Metal contains free electrons (1); free electrons gain kinetic energy when heated (1); electrons move through the metal and collide with other electrons/ions (1); energy transferred along the rod from hot end to cold end (1).

question: Explain how convection currents transfer thermal energy in a liquid.
mark_scheme: Liquid near heat source warms up (1); particles move faster and spread apart — liquid becomes less dense (1); less dense liquid rises (1); cooler, denser liquid sinks to replace it (1); this sets up a convection current that transfers energy throughout the liquid (1) — any four.

question: A 5 kg block of copper is heated from 25°C to 125°C. The specific heat capacity of copper is 385 J/kg°C. Calculate the energy needed and the power of a heater that would achieve this in 5 minutes.
Describe the energy transfers that take place when a catapult fires a stone into the air.
mark_scheme: Chemical energy in muscles transferred to elastic potential energy in the stretched catapult (1); elastic potential energy transferred to kinetic energy of the stone on release (1); kinetic energy transferred to gravitational potential energy as stone rises (1); some energy wasted as thermal/sound energy throughout (1).

question: A light bulb has an efficiency of 0.15 (15%). Calculate the useful light energy output if 300 J of electrical energy is supplied, and explain what happens to the remaining energy.
mark_scheme: Useful light output = efficiency × input = 0.15 × 300 = 45 J (1); remaining energy = 300 − 45 = 255 J (1); wasted as thermal energy / heat (1); dissipated to the surroundings (1).

question: Evaluate solar panels as an energy resource for homes in the United Kingdom. Include economic and environmental considerations.
mark_scheme: Advantage: renewable — will not run out (1); no greenhouse gas emissions during use (1); reduces electricity bills / excess can be sold back to the grid (1); disadvantage: intermittent — only generates in daylight / reduced output in cloudy UK weather (1); high initial installation cost (1); manufacturing panels has environmental impact (1) — any four.

question: A car travelling at 20 m/s has a mass of 1200 kg. Calculate its kinetic energy and explain what happens to this energy when the car brakes to a stop.
mark_scheme: Ek = ½mv² = 0.5 × 1200 × 20² = 0.5 × 1200 × 400 (1) = 240 000 J (1); brakes apply friction force to wheels (1); kinetic energy transferred to thermal energy in brakes/surroundings (1).

question: Describe how thermal energy is transferred by infrared radiation. State two factors that affect the rate of radiation from a surface.
mark_scheme: Infrared radiation is emitted by all objects above absolute zero (1); transferred as electromagnetic waves — no medium required (1); darker/matt surfaces are better emitters than shiny/light surfaces (1); rate of radiation increases with temperature (1); surface area also affects total rate of emission (1) — any four.

question: A 2 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5 m. Calculate its gravitational potential energy at the top (g = 10 N/kg) and its maximum speed just before it hits the ground, assuming no air resistance.
mark_scheme: GPE = mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J (1); at the bottom all GPE converted to KE: ½mv² = 100 (1); v² = 200/2 = 100; v = 10 m/s (1); correct working shown (1).

question: Explain how a hydroelectric power station generates electricity, including the energy transfers involved.
mark_scheme: Water stored at height has gravitational potential energy (1); water falls through pipes/turbines (1); GPE transferred to kinetic energy of water/turbine (1); turbine drives a generator converting kinetic energy to electrical energy (1).

question: Explain the difference between insulating a building to reduce heat loss and using a more efficient boiler. Why are both strategies useful for reducing energy consumption?
mark_scheme: Insulation reduces the rate of heat loss through walls/roof/windows (1); less energy needed to maintain indoor temperature (1); more efficient boiler transfers a greater proportion of fuel's chemical energy to heat (1); less fuel wasted — lower bills and emissions (1); both together give greater overall reduction in energy use than either alone (1) — any four.

question: Explain how conduction, convection and radiation each transfer thermal energy. Give one example of each.
mark_scheme: Conduction: energy transferred through vibrations of particles / free electron collisions (1); e.g. metal spoon in hot drink (1); convection: warmer, less dense fluid rises and cooler, denser fluid sinks setting up currents (1); e.g. central heating radiator warming a room (1); radiation: energy transferred by infrared electromagnetic waves with no medium needed (1); e.g. warmth felt from the Sun (1) — any five.

question: A wind turbine produces 8 MW of electrical power when the wind delivers 20 MW of kinetic energy to its blades. Calculate the efficiency of the turbine, and explain two reasons why it cannot be 100% efficient.
mark_scheme: Efficiency = useful output/total input = 8/20 = 0.4 or 40% (1); correct working shown (1); energy wasted as sound/vibration (1); energy wasted due to friction in bearings/gearbox (1); some wind passes through without transferring energy to blades (1) — any five.

question: Explain why water is used as a coolant in car engines and why it is also used in central heating systems. Refer to its specific heat capacity in your answer.
mark_scheme: Water has a very high specific heat capacity (4200 J/kg°C) (1); can absorb large amounts of energy with small temperature rise (1); effective at carrying heat away from engine preventing overheating (1); in central heating: water stores large amounts of energy at the boiler (1); releases energy gradually to radiators around the house (1).

question: Evaluate geothermal energy as a source of electricity. Consider its advantages, disadvantages and suitability for the UK.
mark_scheme: Geothermal: heat from underground rocks used to produce steam to drive turbines (1); advantage: renewable — heat from Earth's interior is effectively unlimited (1); no greenhouse gas emissions (1); reliable — not dependent on weather (1); disadvantage: only viable in geologically active areas (volcanoes/hot springs) (1); UK has limited geothermal resources (1); high drilling costs (1) — any five.

question: A pendulum swings from one side to the other. Describe the energy transfers at each stage of the swing, and explain why the pendulum eventually comes to rest.
mark_scheme: At maximum height: all gravitational potential energy, zero kinetic energy (1); as it swings down: GPE transferred to kinetic energy (1); at lowest point: all kinetic energy, zero GPE (1); as it swings up the other side: KE transferred back to GPE (1); pendulum gradually slows because air resistance and friction at pivot transfer energy to thermal energy (1).

question: Explain how a coal-fired power station generates electricity. Include all the energy transfers and one environmental impact.
mark_scheme: Coal (chemical energy) burned — chemical energy transferred to thermal energy (1); thermal energy heats water to produce steam (1); steam drives a turbine — thermal/kinetic energy transferred (1); turbine connected to generator — kinetic energy transferred to electrical energy (1); environmental impact: combustion produces CO₂ which is a greenhouse gas causing global warming (1).

question: A 4 kg block of steel (c = 500 J/kg°C) and a 4 kg block of aluminium (c = 900 J/kg°C) are both heated by a 200 W heater for 10 minutes. Calculate the temperature rise of each block and explain which is better for storing thermal energy.
mark_scheme: Energy = Pt = 200 × 600 = 120 000 J (1); ΔT (steel) = E/(mc) = 120 000/(4 × 500) = 60°C (1); ΔT (aluminium) = 120 000/(4 × 900) = 33.3°C (1); aluminium has smaller temperature rise for same energy input (1); aluminium stores more energy per degree so is better for thermal storage (1).

question: A vacuum flask is designed to keep drinks hot or cold. Explain how its design reduces thermal energy transfer by conduction, convection and radiation.
mark_scheme: Double-walled glass construction with vacuum between walls (1); vacuum prevents conduction and convection as no particles to carry energy (1); silvered inner surfaces reflect infrared radiation back into the flask (1); reduces radiation losses (1); stopper/lid prevents convection at the top (1).

question: Evaluate the use of tidal barrages to generate electricity. In your answer include advantages, disadvantages and compare with wind power.
mark_scheme: Tidal: uses kinetic energy of tidal water to drive turbines (1); advantage: predictable and reliable — tides follow regular patterns (1); no fuel costs / no greenhouse gas emissions (1); disadvantage: very high construction costs (1); disrupts marine ecosystems / estuary habitats (1); wind: cheaper to build and more widespread (1); disadvantage: intermittent — unpredictable (1) — any five.

question: A student measures the efficiency of an electric motor lifting a load. Describe the steps the student would take, including what measurements to make and how to calculate efficiency. Suggest two sources of error.
mark_scheme: Measure mass of load and height lifted (1); use GPE = mgh to find useful output energy (1); measure electrical energy input using joulemeter or E = Pt (1); efficiency = useful output/total input (1); sources of error: energy wasted as heat in motor (1); friction in pulley/string (1); energy used to lift the string itself (1) — any five.

question: Explain why biomass is considered a renewable energy resource but still has environmental concerns. Discuss whether it should be considered 'carbon neutral'.
mark_scheme: Biomass is renewable because new plants can be grown to replace those burned (1); plants absorb CO₂ during photosynthesis (1); burning biomass releases CO₂ — theoretically balanced (1); but energy used in growing, harvesting, transporting adds extra carbon emissions (1); deforestation for biomass reduces CO₂ absorption (1); not truly carbon neutral in practice (1) — any five.

question: Explain what specific heat capacity means and why coastal areas have a more moderate climate than inland areas. Include calculations to support your answer given that water has c = 4200 J/kg°C and land has c = 800 J/kg°C.
mark_scheme: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C (1); water has a much higher specific heat capacity than land (1); for same energy input, land heats up and cools down much faster than water: e.g. 1 kg of water needs 4200 J per °C but land needs only 800 J (1); sea acts as a thermal reservoir — absorbs heat in summer and releases it slowly in winter (1); coastal areas stay warmer in winter and cooler in summer compared to inland (1); inland areas have greater seasonal temperature variation (1).

question: A house loses heat through its walls, roof, windows and floors. Evaluate different methods of reducing heat loss from a house. For each method, explain the mechanism of heat transfer it reduces and assess its effectiveness and cost.
mark_scheme: Loft insulation: traps air reducing convection and conduction through roof (1); inexpensive and effective as most heat lost through roof (1); cavity wall insulation: fills air gap in walls reducing convection currents (1); effective but more expensive to install (1); double glazing: air/vacuum gap between panes reduces conduction (1); costly but also reduces draughts and noise (1); draught-proofing: reduces convection through gaps (1); cheap and easy to install (1) — any six.

question: A bungee jumper of mass 70 kg jumps from a platform 50 m above the ground. Explain all the energy transfers from the moment of jumping to when the jumper momentarily comes to rest. Use g = 10 N/kg. Include numerical values where appropriate.
mark_scheme: Initial GPE = mgh = 70 × 10 × 50 = 35 000 J (1); as jumper falls, GPE transferred to kinetic energy (1); cord begins to stretch — KE transferred to elastic potential energy in cord (1); at lowest point, KE = 0, energy in GPE + elastic PE stores (1); some energy transferred to thermal energy due to air resistance throughout fall (1); at lowest point, sum of GPE and elastic PE equals original GPE minus energy wasted (1).

question: A remote island community currently relies on diesel generators for electricity. Evaluate whether they should switch to a combination of wind and solar power with battery storage, considering reliability, environmental impact, and cost.
mark_scheme: Diesel: reliable but burns fossil fuel producing CO₂ (1); fuel must be imported increasing cost and supply risk (1); wind: free fuel and low emissions once built (1); intermittent — may not generate in calm weather (1); solar: free fuel, no emissions (1); only generates in daylight, reduced in cloudy conditions (1); battery storage: allows excess energy to be stored for use when generation is low (1); combination increases reliability compared to single source (1); high upfront cost but lower long-term running costs (1) — any six.

question: Explain the concept of energy dissipation and why it means useful energy is always less than input energy. Use the example of a car engine to illustrate your answer, and suggest how the efficiency of a car can be improved.
mark_scheme: Energy dissipation means energy spreading out into the surroundings as thermal energy (1); once dissipated, energy cannot be recovered for useful work (1); car engine: chemical energy in fuel converted to kinetic energy (1); but energy wasted as heat in engine, exhaust gases, friction (1); typical car engine is only ~25–35% efficient (1); improvements: streamlined bodywork reduces air resistance (1); lubricate moving parts to reduce friction (1); regenerative braking recovers kinetic energy (1); use lighter materials (1) — any six.

question: Evaluate the environmental, social and economic impacts of building a large wind farm offshore. Consider impacts during construction, operation and decommissioning.
mark_scheme: Construction: ships and equipment use fossil fuels releasing emissions (1); disruption to seabed and marine life (1); Operation: no greenhouse gas emissions (1); noise impact on wildlife / nearby residents minimal offshore (1); visual impact minimal if far offshore (1); provides jobs in construction and maintenance (1); decommissioning: turbines must be removed responsibly / materials can be recycled (1); overall: much lower lifecycle emissions than fossil fuels (1); helps reduce dependence on imported fuels (1) — any six.

question: Explain in detail how a thermal power station converts stored chemical energy in coal into electrical energy. Describe the energy transfers at each stage and identify where energy is wasted.
mark_scheme: Coal burned in furnace — chemical energy to thermal energy (1); thermal energy heats water in boiler — steam produced (1); high-pressure steam drives turbine blades — thermal/pressure energy to kinetic energy (1); turbine connected to generator — kinetic energy to electrical energy (1); energy wasted as heat in furnace/boiler (1); energy wasted in turbine due to friction (1); exhaust steam condensed — heat released to environment (1); overall efficiency typically 30–40% (1) — any six.

question: The UK government is planning to increase the use of hydrogen as a fuel. Evaluate hydrogen as an energy carrier, considering how it is produced, stored, used and its environmental impact compared to fossil fuels.
mark_scheme: Hydrogen produced by electrolysis of water (1); if powered by renewable energy, production is carbon-free — 'green hydrogen' (1); if produced from natural gas, releases CO₂ — 'grey hydrogen' (1); combustion of hydrogen only produces water — no direct emissions (1); storage challenge: hydrogen is highly flammable and difficult to store safely under pressure (1); fuel cells can convert hydrogen directly to electricity efficiently (1); environmental benefit only if renewable energy used in production (1); could replace natural gas in heating / transport (1) — any six.

question: State four different types of energy store.
mark_scheme: Any four from: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, chemical, thermal, nuclear, electrostatic, magnetic (1 mark for each pair of two named, so any 2 for 2 marks — adjust: any two stores named for 1 mark each).

question: Explain the difference between energy and power.
mark_scheme: Energy is the total amount stored or transferred, measured in joules (1); power is the rate of energy transfer — how quickly energy is transferred — measured in watts (1).

question: Give two ways of increasing the efficiency of a device.
mark_scheme: Any two: lubricate moving parts to reduce friction (1); streamline to reduce air resistance (1); insulate to reduce heat loss (1); use more efficient components (1).

question: State two advantages and one disadvantage of wind power.
mark_scheme: Advantages: renewable / will not run out (1); no greenhouse gas emissions during operation (1); disadvantage: any valid — intermittent, visual/noise pollution, wildlife impact (1) — two advantages for 2 marks.

question: Describe the energy transfers when a stretched elastic band is released and propels a ball upwards.
mark_scheme: Elastic potential energy in the band is transferred to kinetic energy of the ball on release (1); as the ball rises, kinetic energy is transferred to gravitational potential energy (1).

question: Give the equation for power in terms of energy and time, and state the unit of power.
mark_scheme: Power = energy ÷ time / P = E/t (1); unit is the watt (W) (1).

question: State two non-renewable energy resources and give one environmental disadvantage of each.
mark_scheme: Any two: coal → produces CO₂ / acid rain pollutants (1); oil → produces CO₂ / risk of oil spills (1); natural gas → produces CO₂ (1); nuclear → produces radioactive waste (1).

question: Name the type of energy store that increases when an object is lifted higher above the ground.
mark_scheme: Gravitational potential energy (1); GPE increases because the object is at a greater height — GPE = mgh (1).

question: Give the equation for efficiency and state the maximum possible value of efficiency.
mark_scheme: Efficiency = useful output energy / total input energy (1); maximum efficiency = 1 (or 100%) — no real device can be 100% efficient (1).

question: Describe how a solar cell generates electricity.
mark_scheme: A solar cell converts light energy (from the Sun) directly into electrical energy (1); when light falls on the cell, it causes electrons to flow, generating a current (1).

question: State what is meant by the term 'dissipation of energy' and give one example.
mark_scheme: Dissipation means energy spreading out into the surroundings in a less useful form, usually as thermal energy (1); example: a light bulb wastes energy as heat / friction in a motor causes energy to be lost as heat (1).

question: Explain the energy transfers in a pendulum as it swings from one side to the other. Include what happens to the energy if the pendulum eventually stops.
mark_scheme: At the highest point of the swing, the pendulum has maximum gravitational potential energy and zero kinetic energy (1); as it swings down, GPE is transferred to kinetic energy — maximum KE at the lowest point (1); as it swings up the other side, KE is transferred back to GPE; the pendulum slows because air resistance and friction at the pivot continuously transfer small amounts of energy to thermal energy in the surroundings (1).

question: Explain why transmitting electricity at high voltage across the National Grid reduces energy losses.
mark_scheme: The same power can be transmitted at high voltage and low current (since P = IV) (1); power wasted as heat in cables is given by P = I²R, so lower current means much less energy is wasted as heat (1); step-up transformers increase voltage before transmission; step-down transformers reduce voltage to a safe level for homes (1).

question: Describe an experiment to measure the efficiency of an electric motor lifting a weight.
mark_scheme: Measure the mass of the weight and the height it is lifted (1); calculate useful output energy: GPE = mgh (1); measure electrical energy input using a joulemeter or by calculating E = P × t; efficiency = GPE gained / electrical energy input (1).

question: Explain how a hydroelectric power station generates electricity, including all the energy transfers.
mark_scheme: Water stored in a reservoir at height has gravitational potential energy (1); water flows down through pipes and drives turbines — GPE transferred to kinetic energy of the turbines (1); turbines are connected to generators — kinetic energy is transferred to electrical energy (1).

question: Compare wind power and solar power as energy resources. Include reliability and environmental impact.
mark_scheme: Both are renewable and produce no greenhouse gases during operation (1); wind power: intermittent — only generates when wind blows; suitable for windy coastal/highland areas; may affect wildlife (1); solar power: only generates in daylight; less effective in cloudy regions like the UK; manufacturing panels has environmental cost (1).

question: Explain what happens to the kinetic energy of a car when the brakes are applied. Include the energy transfer and the effect on the brakes.
mark_scheme: When brakes are applied, friction between brake pads and discs creates a force opposing motion (1); kinetic energy of the car is transferred to thermal energy in the brakes and surroundings (1); the brakes heat up — over repeated heavy braking, this can cause brake fade as the brakes become too hot to be effective (1).

question: Describe how the power consumption of a household appliance can be used to calculate the cost of using it for a given time.
mark_scheme: Convert power to kilowatts (kW) (1); multiply by time in hours to get energy in kilowatt-hours (kWh): Energy = P(kW) × t(hours) (1); multiply by the cost per kWh to find total cost (1).

question: Explain why buildings lose heat more quickly in winter and describe two measures that reduce this heat loss.
mark_scheme: Greater temperature difference between inside and outside in winter increases the rate of heat transfer (1); loft insulation traps air in fibres, reducing convection and conduction through the roof (1); double glazing reduces conduction through windows — air or vacuum gap between panes acts as insulator (1).

question: Explain the advantages of offshore wind farms compared with onshore wind farms.
mark_scheme: Offshore winds are stronger and more consistent, increasing electricity output (1); turbines are further from homes, reducing noise and visual impact concerns (1); more space available offshore so larger arrays can be built; however, offshore installation and maintenance is more expensive (1).

question: Compare the gravitational potential energy of two objects: Object A has a mass of 2 kg at a height of 5 m, and Object B has a mass of 5 kg at a height of 2 m. Use g = 10 N/kg.
mark_scheme: GPE(A) = mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J (1); GPE(B) = mgh = 5 × 10 × 2 = 100 J (1); both objects have equal gravitational potential energy despite having different masses and heights (1).

question: Explain why a filament light bulb is less efficient than an LED bulb, and calculate the efficiency of a filament bulb that transfers 5 J of light energy from 50 J of electrical energy.
mark_scheme: A filament bulb converts most electrical energy to heat rather than light — wasteful (1); an LED converts more electrical energy to light with less heat waste (1); efficiency = useful output / total input = 5/50 = 0.1 or 10% (1).

question: Describe what a Sankey diagram shows and explain how it represents wasted energy.
mark_scheme: A Sankey diagram shows all energy transfers from a device — input and all outputs (1); the width of each arrow is proportional to the amount of energy it represents (1); wasted energy is shown as arrows leaving in unintended directions, usually thermal energy to the surroundings (1).
